title: Accurate Large-sample Uncertainty Quantification using Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: Existing tuning rules degrade as batch size grows, while our discrete-time theory keeps covariance error low across regimes.
layout: 1 panel line plot, error versus batch size, shaded confidence bands, legend top-left
description: A single line plot with batch size (0 to 512) on the x-axis and Frobenius-norm error between the sandwich covariance and the estimated covariance on the y-axis (about 10 to 60). Dashed grid lines run behind the data. A legend at top-left lists three methods. CT is a solid blue line with circle markers. LR+WS is an orange dashed line with square markers. DQ+exact (this paper) is a green dash-dot line with triangle markers. Each line has a translucent shaded band. The orange baseline stays high at about 41 to 54. The blue baseline starts near 12 and climbs sharply past batch size 256 to about 46. The green line stays lowest, rising only to about 19. The eye goes first to the widening gap between the green line and the other two at large batch sizes.
caption: Misspecified linear regression with heteroskedastic noise. Data are generated according to $y_{n} \dist \Norm(x_{n}^{\top}\theta_{\star}, 1+\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2})$, where $\theta_{\star} \dist \Norm(0, I_{D})$ is fixed and $x_{n} \distiid \Norm(0, I_{D})$. A linear model is fitted using constant-step-size SGD. $\mathcal{S}_{\star} = \mathcal{J}_{\star}^{-1} \mathcal{I}_{\star} \mathcal{J}_{\star}^{-1}$: sandwich covariance; $\hat{\mathcal{S}}$: covariance obtained under step-size tuning rules derived from different theories.
abstract: Tuning algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) for approximate sampling and uncertainty quantification remains challenging, particularly in the practically relevant settings when the batch size is large or the model is misspecified. Existing theory that provides tuning guidance relies on continuous-time limits or strong statistical assumptions, which can become quantitatively inaccurate in these regimes. We address these shortcomings by proposing new discrete-time approximations to SG(L)D with and without momentum, which enables accurate predictions of the stationary covariance, iterate average covariance, and integrated autocorrelation time. Moreover, we prove quantitative, non-asymptotic error bounds showing that these estimates are sufficiently accurate for practical tuning and uncertainty quantification. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our theory yields improved tuning guidance across a range of models and data-generating distributions where existing approaches fail, including when using the $Î²$-divergence rather than log-loss to obtain statistically robust inferences.
